requirement: Habeas MUST identify a Rust item by the pair of its `rust_file`, following the path rules in {cite}`requirements.ci.schema`, and a `rust_item` selector derived from a `syn` parse of that file. The selector MUST describe syntactic ancestry within the file and MUST NOT resolve Rust modules across files or use line numbers as identity. Named items MUST use kind-and-name segments such as `fn[run]` and `struct[Packet]`. Impl segments MUST distinguish inherent from trait impls using their syntactic self type and optional trait path. Otherwise identical selectors MUST have deterministic source-order disambiguators. A `use` declaration MUST have a positional selector `use#N`, where N is its one-based position among sibling `use` declarations; its import target MUST NOT form part of the selector. Other items without a suitable name MUST have a kind and positional disambiguator. Selector spelling MUST be documented and reversible when names or types contain delimiter characters.
rationale:
**Implementation (`src/rust_items.rs`)**
- `parse_items` builds selectors from a `syn::parse_file` parse of one file. `ItemCollector` walks items, impl items, trait items and foreign items, keeping a parent stack. Selectors therefore express syntactic ancestry within that file. Nothing resolves `mod x;` across files, and line numbers are never part of identity. Line and byte data are kept as separate `RustItem` fields.
- Named items use `kind[name]` segments through `named`. This covers `fn`, `struct`, `enum`, `trait`, `mod`, `const`, `static`, `type`, `union`, `macro_rules` and `extern-crate`. Foreign blocks become `extern[ABI]`.
- Impl segments are `impl[SelfType]` for inherent impls and `impl[SelfType/Trait]` for trait impls. Both use the syntactic source text of the self type and trait path.
- Items that would otherwise share a selector are grouped by `(parent, base)` and sorted by byte start. They get `#N` suffixes in source order, which is deterministic.
- `use` always yields `use#N`, with no import target in the selector. `ordinal_always` makes this one-based position among sibling `use` items apply even when there is only one.
- Unnamed items (macro invocations and unknown or verbatim items) get a kind plus a positional `#N`, for example `macro#1` and `item#1`.
- `escape_segment` percent-encodes `%`, `[`, `]`, `/`, `#` and whitespace as UTF-8 bytes. Together with the documentation, this makes the spelling reversible. `md/reference.md` (around line 382) documents the spelling, the examples, the duplicate `#N` suffixes and the percent-encoding.
- The helper structs and functions carry `{impl}` references. The extra behavior (line ranges and attached comments) is marked with `{impl}` for `requirements.ci.rust_item_inputs`. The only oddity is unused `_name` and `_is_function` parameters on `add`, which is harmless.
- Rust-file path handling is done by callers (`inputs.rs`, `add_input.rs`) under the `requirements.ci.schema` rules.

**Tests**
- `selectors_name_syntactic_ancestry_and_duplicates` is marked `{test}` for this requirement and the examples `selector_nested`, `selector_impl_and_trait`, `selector_inline_and_foreign`, `selector_duplicate_names` and `selector_use`. It asserts these selectors:
  - `use#1` and `use#2`
  - `mod[local]/fn[run]` and `mod[external]`
  - `impl[Thing]/fn[run]` and `impl[Thing/Trait]/fn[run]`
  - `impl[%5Bu8;%204%5D]/fn[edge]`, which exercises delimiter and whitespace escaping
  - `trait[Trait]/fn[read]`, `extern[C]/fn[puts]` and `fn[outer]/fn[inner]`
  - `fn[repeated]#1` and `fn[repeated]#2`
- `tests/commands.rs` additionally exercises selectors through the CLI (`selector_same_line` and `selector_raw_lines`).
- Minor test gaps remain: escaping of `/`, `#` and `%` is not asserted, and neither is `macro#N` or `item#N` for unnamed items. These follow the same code paths as the tested cases, so they do not undermine the judgment.

The requirement is implemented completely, marked completely, documented and reasonably covered by tests.

A requirement or example evidence file at `evidence/<full-name>.json` MUST be a JSON object with exactly `requirement` or `example`, `determination`, `rationale`, and `inputs`. The definition text and rationale MUST be nonempty strings, `determination` MUST use one of the outcomes defined by {cite}`requirements.ci.outcomes`, and `inputs` MUST be an array. Every evidence input MUST have exactly one of four forms: a file-range input with `file`, `line_start`, `line_end`, and `text`; a Rust-item input with `rust_file`, `rust_item`, and `text`; a requirements input with `requirements`, `matches`, and `text`; or a definition input with `definition` and `text`. File paths MUST resolve to permitted inputs under {cite}`requirements.ci.input_containment`. Project-local paths SHOULD be recorded relative to the project for portability; absolute and parent-relative paths MAY be used when their resolved targets are permitted. Line numbers MUST be positive integers, `matches` MUST be an array of distinct full definition names, and `text` MUST be a nonempty array of strings.

Habeas MUST identify a Rust item by the pair of its `rust_file`, following the path rules in {cite}`requirements.ci.schema`, and a `rust_item` selector derived from a `syn` parse of that file. The selector MUST describe syntactic ancestry within the file and MUST NOT resolve Rust modules across files or use line numbers as identity. Named items MUST use kind-and-name segments such as `fn[run]` and `struct[Packet]`. Impl segments MUST distinguish inherent from trait impls using their syntactic self type and optional trait path. Otherwise identical selectors MUST have deterministic source-order disambiguators. A `use` declaration MUST have a positional selector `use#N`, where N is its one-based position among sibling `use` declarations; its import target MUST NOT form part of the selector. Other items without a suitable name MUST have a kind and positional disambiguator. Selector spelling MUST be documented and reversible when names or types contain delimiter characters.

In Markdown, escaped roles and role-looking text in inline code, fenced code, or raw HTML MUST remain literal and MUST NOT count as references. A `{req}` directive inside a fenced code example and a legacy inline `{req}` role MUST NOT define a requirement.

The book preprocessor MUST escape requirement names and link targets when inserting badge HTML. It MUST encode badge label and message text in Shields.io URL path components so punctuation cannot change the badge URL structure.
In `src/lib.rs`, `fn outer() { fn inner() {} }` gives the selectors `fn[outer]` and `fn[outer]/fn[inner]`. {cite}`requirements.references.rust_item_selectors`

In `src/lib.rs`, a method `run` in `impl Thing` has selector `impl[Thing]/fn[run]`; a method `run` in `impl Trait for Thing` has selector `impl[Thing/Trait]/fn[run]`; and a method `read` declared in `trait Read` has selector `trait[Read]/fn[read]`. {cite}`requirements.references.rust_item_selectors`

A function `run` inside an inline `mod local { ... }` in `src/lib.rs` has selector `mod[local]/fn[run]`. A function defined in a separate `src/local.rs` file has a selector within that file, without reconstructing the path of a `mod local;` declaration elsewhere. A foreign function `puts` in an `extern "C"` block has selector `extern[C]/fn[puts]`. {cite}`requirements.references.rust_item_selectors`

Two sibling declarations named `run` in one file, guarded by different `#[cfg]` attributes, have selectors `fn[run]#1` and `fn[run]#2` in source order. Their source line numbers are not part of either selector. {cite}`requirements.references.rust_item_selectors`

For consecutive sibling declarations `use alpha::A;` and `use beta::B;`, the selectors are `use#1` and `use#2`. Changing an import target leaves that declaration's positional selector the same and changes its raw evidence input. A named declaration such as `struct Packet;` instead has selector `struct[Packet]`. {cite}`requirements.references.rust_item_selectors` {cite}`requirements.ci.rust_item_inputs`

For a function preceded by a doc comment, an attribute, and an attached citation comment, a Rust-item input starts at the earliest attached line and ends at the function's final line. Its `text` contains those complete raw source lines. Inserting lines before them changes the displayed range without changing the input. {cite}`requirements.ci.rust_item_inputs`

For `impl Thing { fn run() {} }` on one line, `habeas add-input --for-requirement requirements.foo --rust-item src/lib.rs:1` adds separate inputs for `impl[Thing]` and `impl[Thing]/fn[run]`. Both contain the complete raw line. {cite}`requirements.cli.add_input_rust_item`

Given a requirement `foo.a.bar` and a named example `foo.a.b.bar`, `foo.*.bar` matches both, in that order. A requirements input stores both full names and their complete raw fenced declarations. Adding another matching definition invalidates the existing input. {cite}`requirements.references.definition_globs` {cite}`requirements.ci.requirements_inputs`

Some sources cannot or should not carry a reference themselves, such as a shipped agent skill. A requirement can anchor such a file with `:impl:` or `:test:` option lines immediately after its opening fence; an example can use `:test:`. Each anchor is an edge to the complete file, so that requirement's evidence must contain an input covering every line of it, and changing the file makes the evidence stale. Option lines are not part of the requirement text. Prefer a precise in-source reference whenever one is possible.
The bundled skill MUST explain how to author evidence.

For Rust, Habeas parses first-party source files and requires every explicit function or method, including trait methods and test helpers, to have a requirement or named example reference in an attached comment or its body. Each named example references a requirement. A reference on an enclosing `impl` or module, in a string literal, or only in an evidence input does not cover the function. A Rust source file that cannot be parsed is reported as an error. For a helper with no behavior-specific requirement, agree on an explicit internal-detail requirement scoped to one area, such as `internal.config_parsing`, rather than one catch-all, and mark the helper with `{impl}`. That requirement's review checks that it explains each implementing function's behavior; it cannot justify otherwise unspecified user-visible behavior. {cite}`requirements.references.rust_item_coverage` {cite}`requirements.cli.internal_detail_guidance`

Rust-item selectors use syntactic ancestry within one repository-relative file. Examples include `mod[local]/fn[run]`, `impl[Thing]/fn[run]`, `impl[Thing/Trait]/fn[run]`, `trait[Trait]/fn[read]`, `fn[outer]/fn[inner]`, and positional `use#1`. Duplicate sibling names gain `#1`, `#2`, and so on. Delimiter characters and whitespace within names or impl types use percent-encoded UTF-8 bytes, so spelling can be recovered without resolving modules across files. {cite}`requirements.references.rust_item_selectors`

The test created by `habeas setup` calls `habeas::validate()`. Run `cargo test --workspace` to find missing evidence, false determinations, changed lines, uncovered `{impl}` and `{test}` references, and unreferenced Rust functions. Validation accepts true and FIXME judgments when all other evidence checks pass. FIXME remains visible in status and the book with its recorded references and rationale. These checks are deterministic: they verify the saved evidence without inference or reassessing the reviewer's judgment about documented gaps. The check reports all the errors it finds, with diffs for changed text. Run `mdbook build` to render the book. {cite}`requirements.ci.determination`
Run `habeas status [<selection>]` from within the project to list requirements and named
examples needing attention and their validation findings. FIXME judgments are
- 16 judgments marked FIXME without an issue
Each judgment counts once per issue, even if it repeats that reference. A judgment
with several issues counts in each group; the final group counts judgments with
no recognized issue reference. References may appear in explanatory text or
`FIXME(...)`. Qualified references such as `rust-lang/rust#123` and GitHub issue
URLs are also recognized. Groups with the most affected judgments come first.
Use `--verbose` to list the actual judgments in each group, with their full names,
kinds, and recorded FIXME strings. `--all` shows every matching definition and its
evidence state. Stale or invalid FIXME evidence still reports its validation
findings. Use `habeas info <selection>` to print matching detail pages as Markdown,
including current texts, rationales, inputs, FIXME references, and findings. Both
commands take a definition selection: a full name selects exactly that definition,
and in a glob `*` can span any number of characters, including dots. {cite}`requirements.cli.status` {cite}`requirements.cli.info`
